beats.say: A penny gets you a whole music library. And you never see the bill.
Pick eight CDs for a cent.
Or join the club and pay regular prices.
Or let the next CD ship unless you opt out.
You must buy a minimum number later. Sounds generous.
But it's a negative-option trap: the penny is just a hook.
The cheap entry becomes a contract; the next CD ships and you are billed.
Revenue peaked at $1.4 billion in 1996, then fell to $17 million by 2014.
Bankruptcy filing in August 2015 proved the model collapsed.
A coffee shop gives a free muffin with any drink, unless you cancel.
A gym charges $1 to sign up, then forces a monthly plan.
Because the cheap entry locks you in, the pricier plan seems smart.
If a deal starts with a penny, expect a hidden bill. Follow for more.
